name: Earth-bathing

lead: Earth bathing is a practice from the nature-cure tradition in which people lie in, or are covered with, soil or clay. Its best-known promoter was German naturopath Adolf Just (1859-1936), whose "Return to Nature" movement emphasised clay, fresh air and sunlight.

Supporters connect it with healthy-looking skin and general vitality, in the same way mud baths and clay masks are used in spas. Published research on earth burial itself is minimal; research on mud baths covers areas such as osteoarthritis pain.

paras: Practitioners describe lying on or being covered with moist earth or clay outdoors or in a spa setting for a period of time, sometimes with sun and fresh air as part of a broader naturopathic routine. Mud-bath spas use warm mineral-rich clay mixed with water for about 15 to 20 minutes.

No safety data exist for full-body earth burial. Soil can carry bacteria and fungi, and heat and enclosure carry general risks. Mud-bath therapy in clinical use is warm, controlled and applied in spas.

angle.text: Supporters of earth and clay bathing describe healthier skin and a sense of relaxation. This is a traditional claim from the nature-cure movement and from spa mud bathing.

lead: Earth bathing refers to the practice of lying in, or being covered with, earth or clay for supposed healing, a theme of the nature-cure tradition. Adolf Just (1859-1936), a German naturopath, built his "Return to Nature" ideas around natural food, clean water, fresh air, earthen clay and time outdoors, and founded the Jungborn institute in 1895 [1].

Followers of such practices describe benefits for skin and general wellbeing, an idea shared with mud baths, which are said to promote healthy skin, ease muscle tension and relax [2]. The practice relates to wider spa use of clay.
Research on earth bathing itself is not available; a 2021 systematic review of mud-bath therapy in osteoarthritis concluded it cannot substitute for conventional therapy but may complement it [2].

paras: Adolf Just founded Jungborn in Eckertal in 1895 and, in 1918, a healing-clay society in Blankenburg; his book Kehrt zur Natur zurück! was translated into English in 1903 by Benedict Lust [1]. His approach also included raw vegetarian diet and outdoor living, and he rejected conventional drugs and vaccination, a position for which later writers criticised him [1].

Mud baths soak the body in warm mineral-rich clay or peloid, often from lakes, hot springs or the Dead Sea, usually for 15 to 20 minutes; alleged benefits include improved blood flow, muscle relaxation and healthy skin [2].

No studies found on earth bathing. A 2021 systematic review of mud-bath therapy in osteoarthritis (a related practice) reported possible pain and stiffness relief as an add-on to conventional care [2].
